title: Speech by Commissioner Kadis at the “Climate Action in the Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East: Regional Cooperation Empowered by Science and Innovation” Conference
matched_keywords: Climate; Climate Change; Environment; carbon; climate goals
text:
"Check against delivery"
Excellencies, Distinguished guests, Ladies and gentlemen,
First, I would like to congratulate the Cyprus Institute, the EMME Secretariat and the Deputy Ministry of Research, Innovation and Digital Policy of Cyprus for organising this event, under the aegis of the Cyprus Presidency of the Council of the EU.
It is a privilege to be with you today, both in my role as Commissioner and as a native of Cyprus, a country whose history, like so many in this region, is inseparable from the sea.
The Eastern Mediterranean is a cradle of civilisation, where the fate of millions of people, of so many of our communities, is tied to the health of our seas.
Yet, as climate change unfolds, the very essence of these communities and their reliance on marine resources are jeopardised. Here, in the Eastern Mediterranean, we can clearly see that the climate crisis is an ocean crisis. Our response must be bold and collective.
The Mediterranean Sea is warming much faster than the global average. Marine heatwaves, acidification, and invasive species are already reshaping ecosystems, threatening fisheries, tourism, and coastal communities. The EU's Copernicus Marine Service confirms what our fishers already know: stocks are shifting, catches are declining, and traditional livelihoods are at risk.
Against this background, last year the Commission presented the European Ocean Pact. A comprehensive strategy to better protect the ocean, promote a competitive and sustainable blue economy and support the well-being of people living in coastal areas. I am proud to say that we are now in the process of implementing the objectives of the Ocean Pact.
But to succeed, we need a good understanding of the ocean, our biggest climate regulator. And for this, science and innovation are key.
This is why, this March, President von der Leyen unveiled OceanEye, our European Ocean Observation Initiative. It will be our window on the ocean, and our key to unlocking even more of its secrets.
An essential building block of OceanEye is the Digital Twin Ocean, which is part of our Mission: “Restore our Ocean and Waters”. Set for completion by 2030, it will provide real-time modelling to predict and mitigate climate impacts.
To make these tools more effective, the Commission will present the Ocean Research and Innovation Strategy by the end of this year. This strategy will drive the development of win-win innovative solutions for sustainable development of island and coastal communities, for example through blue carbon sequestration.
Research and innovation are a stabiliser and confidence-building tool in complex geopolitical contexts.
The EU can engage through neutral, rules-based and value-compliant cooperation mechanisms, fully embedded in Horizon Europe and the Partnership for Research and Innovation in the Mediterranean Area (PRIMA).
But data alone is not enough we must turn knowledge into action. As climate change knows no borders, this action must be collective.
The General Fisheries Commission for the Mediterranean (GFCM) proves that science diplomacy and regional collaboration work. Through initiatives like the EU-funded MedSea4Fish, we are improving stock assessments, combating illegal fishing, and promoting sustainable management across shared waters. A healthy, biodiverse ocean equals a stable climate.
Similarly, for aquaculture, the Commission has issued strategic guidelines for a more sustainable and competitive EU aquaculture, while actively working at the international level under the FAO framework. Beyond producing food, aquaculture is also an emerging climate solution. Specific types of farmed seafood can act as a net carbon sink, sequestering carbon as they grow and restore ecosystems, while aquaculture in inland waters can also act as a water “purifier”.
The Pact for the Mediterranean, presented last October, deepens collaboration with our Southern Mediterranean neighbours, prioritising a sustainable blue economy and stronger economic, educational and scientific ties.
I warmly welcome also the Barcelona Convention's important work in supporting our Member States in implementing EU marine environmental laws, and in addressing challenges related to climate change in the Mediterranean Sea.
Further, I would like to remind that the European Commission is currently revising the EU law on the marine environment the Marine Strategy Framework Directive and the Maritime Spatial Planning Directive, as part of the Ocean Pact, which is the legislative component of the Ocean Pact. Our aim is to strengthen the protection of our seas from multiple pressures, including climate challenges.
Finally, the impact of climate change on coastal and island communities and possible solutions will further be addressed in the respective Commission strategies to be adopted this coming June and presented here in Cyprus.
At the same time the European Union continues to engage actively within the UN framework. A key milestone was the entry into force of the Biodiversity Beyond National Jurisdiction (BBNJ) Agreement. The EU plays a catalytic role for the ratification of this important agreement.
This was the moment when we saw that we can achieve our biodiversity, and by extension, our climate goals through collaboration and cooperation in seas beyond national jurisdiction.
Ladies and gentlemen, the Eastern Mediterranean is at a crossroads. As we deal with the effects of climate change that defy borders and geopolitics, it is clear that we must tackle this challenge together.
In this context, I would like to congratulate the Government of the Republic of Cyprus, the Cyprus Institute and all the contributors to the EMME Climate Change Initiative, which promotes and coordinates regional climate action, based on robust scientific data.
Science and innovation can help us to forge pathways to resilience and preserve our marine ecosystems and communities. Together through ambition and collaboration we can secure a resilient, productive, and sustainable ocean that benefits not only this generation, but also those that will follow.

title: Video message by Commissioner Šuica at the Cyprus Institute Conference on "Climate Action in the Eastern Mediterranean and Middle East: Regional Cooperation Empowered by Science and Innovation"
matched_keywords: Climate; commitments; energy; fossil fuel; renewable energy
text:
"Check against delivery"
Dear friends,
I want to thank the Cypriot Presidency of the Council for this very timely conference on climate action.
Our whole region – from Europe to the Middle East – is going through a crisis.
With every passing day, we see more clearly that the consequences of war in the Middle East will be long-term.
Fossil fuel prices will remain high.
And dependence on their volatility will remain a serious constraint.
As serious as the growing climate disasters that affect our economies and destroy lives and livelihoods across our countries.
Just last summer, climate extremes across Europe cost more than 40 billion euro in economic losses.
We must flip this script.
And the Mediterranean has precisely the means for us to do it.
The southern Mediterranean holds some of the world's most abundant and cost-competitive renewable energy resources – 30% to 40% cheaper than in Europe.
Which is why the Pact for the Mediterranean, our flagship regional cooperation initiative, focuses on developing these resources – through the Trans-Mediterranean Renewable Energy and Clean Tech – T-MED, for short.
T-MED is supporting and de-risking investment in renewables.
We want our public money to act as a multiplier that unlocks much more private investment.
Because climate finance is often a big obstacle to concrete action.
In addition, we are working with our partners to lay the groundwork for these investments to flourish.
Take Egypt, for example.
Two years ago, we signed a Strategic and Comprehensive Partnership.
And we are already seeing private investment commitments to the tune of 49 billion euros.
From clean hydrogen to digital, to finance, to education.
This is how we create reliable partnerships for mutual profit.
Building clean and renewables-based economies will take time.
But the opportunities are too great to ignore.
Because the science is clear.
These challenges will not go away – and we must address them.
Just as the title of this conference states:
Doing the fundamental work of regional cooperation empowered by science and innovation.
I look forward to reading the important conclusions of your work.
Thank you.

title: VIDEO: What is the value of a tree?
text:
As we face increasing environmental challenges, understanding the value of a tree is crucial, not just as a commodity but also for nature.
What's a tree actually worth, though?
If you're thinking about the price of a plank of wood or a sheet of paper, then you're missing its real value.
A tree is worth so much more, whether it's the protection it provides from the wind, the reduction in our risk of flooding by preventing soil erosion, or the fact that a complex web of birds, insects, and fungi relies on a single trunk for a home and therefore survival.
Understanding all of this - and more - is key to understanding nature itself.

title: A Living Planet for Future Generations: From awareness to activism
matched_keywords: Climate; Climate Change; Environment; carbon; energy
text:
When retiring at the end of 2016, I trained as a Climate Speaker at Al Gore's The Climate Reality Project in Miami, Florida. Since then, I have given climate presentations to a wide range of audiences, helping people understand the importance of taking action on climate change. I have also served as an ambassador for the European Climate Pact since 2020.
Before retiring, I worked in science and natural resources, focusing on sustainable food systems. Although I had known about climate change for decades, it was only as I became a grandmother that I truly understood the scale of the crisis and its impact on future generations. This led me, together with 11 other women, to co-found the Activist Grannies to encourage older people to take action.
What began as a small initiative has grown into a community of around 7,500 members. We organise seminars, invite experts and politicians, and create spaces for discussion—showing that when older people understand the urgency, they are motivated to act and play an active role in climate solutions.
Across all these roles, I aim to raise awareness about the importance of climate action and nature restoration so we can keep our planet livable for future generations.
How can you support nature restoration?
In your daily life:
- If you own land, consider letting part of it grow naturally—lawns may look neat, but they support far less biodiversity.
- Eat less red meat. Beef production alone uses around half of the Earth’s agricultural land, much of which could otherwise support forests and natural ecosystems, improving carbon storage and biodiversity.
- Buy less. Consuming less helps reduce pressure on nature and supports a more sustainable future.
In your community:
- Start or join a group that organises seminars and events to encourage citizens to support nature restoration. We have seen that many older people are eager to take action. They have both the time and concern for future generations.
- Engage with local decision-makers and encourage them to support restoration efforts.
- You can also organise demonstrations to raise awareness.
At the national level:
- Try to influence decision-making and help prevent new environmental harm. You can vote for politicians who understand the value of nature at both the local and national levels. Key areas include construction, forest restoration (only about 3% of old forests remain in the EU), and energy solutions.
- Listen to scientists and be critical of actions driven by short-term interests. For example, intensive forest use reduces carbon sinks and contributes to the darkening of lakes in Finland due to heavy drainage.

title: Lessons in Urban Greening
text:
I grew up in a small coastal town in Spain, nestled between pine forests and a striking mountain range. This close contact with nature from an early age shaped my view of the importance of conserving our environment. It’s one of the reasons I pursued environmental sciences and specialised in conservation biology.
Today, as part of the team at the Royal Botanical Garden, I coordinate projects like LIFE-myBUILDINGisGREEN. Our mission is to renaturalise our cities, harnessing the profound benefits of biodiversity to solve modern urban challenges.
Across three pilot schools in Solana de los Barros (Spain), Évora, and Porto (Portugal), we implemented 19 Nature-Based Solutions (NBS) designed to help infrastructure adapt to extreme heat and erratic rainfall. By introducing green roofs, living façades, shaded pergolas, and permeable pavements, we transformed over 13,600 m² of urban space.
The results were more than just aesthetic, they were transformative:
- Temperature control: In our Spanish pilot, surface temperatures on exposed walls dropped by more than 20°C. Indoor temperatures fell by 4 to 6°C, staying comfortably below 27°C even in the height of September.
- Energy efficiency: Cooling-related electricity use decreased by over 11%, proving that nature is a powerful ally in energy conservation.
- Water management: Rainwater runoff plummeted from 21.5% to just 3.37%, significantly easing the pressure on municipal drainage systems.
- Biodiversity boost: Life returned to the classroom. We recorded over 25 new species in Porto and a staggering 77 in Solana de los Barros.
Practical insights for urban greening
Based on my experience with LIFE-myBUILDINGisGREEN, here is how we can bring these benefits to any building:
- Target the hot spots: Focus on the areas with the highest solar gain, such as south-facing façades and courtyards. A simple climbing plant on a trellis or well-placed trees provide shade exactly where it’s needed.
- Work with the seasons: Use deciduous species. They offer lush shade in the summer but shed their leaves in winter, allowing the sun to naturally warm the building when it’s cold.
- Prioritise local resilience: Choose hardy, native species suited to your local climate. Long-term success depends on how well a plant fits its environment, not just its initial visual appeal.
- Think holistically: Combine planting with permeable surfaces and rainwater harvesting. This dual-action approach manages heat and water simultaneously while supporting local wildlife.
- Start small and scalable: At a household level, don't feel pressured to install a full green roof immediately. Start with quick wins like climbers on lightweight structures or vegetated joints in outdoor paving.
- Patience is key: Nature-Based Solutions require an establishment phase. Plants need time to settle and mature. The true impact of your work will grow more impressive every year.

title: My Verdederos Journey: 6 years, 31 countries, 28 tons of waste
text:
At Verdederos, we believe that regardless of where you are from, you can play an active role in nature conservation. Through our projects, workshops and cleanup events, we promote the idea that anyone can play an active role in nature conservation.
We always say that no matter where you are or where you are from, you can positively impact our surroundings. Our main tool is social media, specifically Instagram, to connect with people all over the world to turn digital inspiration into real-world impact.
So far, we have organised over 150 events in 31 countries. Together with more than 3,000 volunteers, we have removed over 28 tons of waste from the environment.
One of our recent highlights was Hitch for Change, a 50-day hitchhiking journey through 12 EU countries. We combined sustainable travel with direct action, organising cleanups in every country by joining forces with local organisations and tourists alike.
This grew into Tour de Impacto RD 2026, a 30-day cleanup tour across the Dominican Republic. This project reached over 5 million views on social media and sparked a national conversation through radio, TV, and podcasts, proving that change is possible when a community finds its voice.
How you can support nature restoration
Many people care deeply about nature but feel their individual actions are a drop in the ocean. My goal is to show that nature restoration is built on exactly these small, consistent steps. As an European Climate Pact Ambassador, I’ve seen how individual actions can inspire wider change.
At the local level:
- Start small: Organise a cleanup with friends, family, or coworkers. Choose a spot that matters to you personally.
- Keep it simple: You only need basic equipment like gloves, bags, and antibacterial gel.
- Measure your impact: Use a luggage scale to weigh what you have collected. Sharing these tangible numbers on social media is a powerful way to motivate others to join next time.
In your daily life:
- Reduce & rethink: Limit single-use plastics at a pace that feels comfortable for you.
- Be conscious: Check what you’re throwing away and ask if it could have been reduced or reused.
Through community:
- Lead by example: We often say that everyone is an influencer within their own social circles, and nothing motivates more than leading by example. Encourage people with a smile. Be patient and do not judge.
- Stay inspired: Talk about sustainability and join local events to build a network of like-minded people. Mutual motivation is the secret to long-term consistency.
Every action counts
Through Verdederos, I learned that you do not need to be an expert to make a difference. For example, I studied medicine, not environmental science. I started simply as a "preoccupied citizen" and discovered thousands of others who felt the same but just needed a little push.
After six years, I am still amazed at how one positive action ripples into something much larger. Most importantly, do not get discouraged. If you start alone or people tell you it is not worth it, keep going. Every piece of trash removed matters. You aren’t alone in this; there are millions of us, and in our connected world, the proof is everywhere.
What is one small environmental change you’ve been thinking about trying lately?

title: Reconnecting Our Health, Food, and Future to the Living Soil
text:
Restoring nature starts from the ground beneath our feet. Healthy soils are essential for food production, water regulation, biodiversity, and climate resilience. Yet we rarely think about soil in our everyday lives.
Nature restoration is not only the responsibility of institutions, scientists, or farmers — citizens across Europe also have a vital role to play. Through simple daily choices, practical actions at home, and collective engagement at the local level, everyone can contribute to restoring soil health.
As an agricultural engineer and European Soil Ambassador, I have chosen to act to raise soil literacy and awareness through an unusual approach: movement. I use my feet to reconnect with the ground beneath us. After working closely with farmers, researchers, and local stakeholders, I came to see soils as the missing link between environmental health, food systems, and human wellbeing.
Since 2025, through an initiative called Enraciné (“Rooted”), I have been running long distances across different regions to meet farmers, scientists, citizens, and young people. Through this project — and my upcoming journey across France in 2026 — I aim to raise awareness by combining field experience with scientific insights, helping people better understand the fundamental role of soils in our health, ecosystems and food systems.
But you don't have to be a marathon runner: Walking, gardening, observing, learning, and sharing knowledge — you can all reconnect with our precious soil. Restoring it often begins with simply taking the time to notice it.
In our gardens: Working with nature
We can actively support soil health, starting in our gardens. Simple practices can boost soil biodiversity and strengthen natural processes.
- Covering the soil with mulch — such as leaves, grass clippings, or wood chips — protects soil life, reduces erosion, and helps retain moisture.
- Composting kitchen and garden waste returns essential organic matter to the soil, improving its structure and fertility.
- Reducing soil disturbance by avoiding deep digging helps preserve fungal networks and soil habitats,
- Planting diverse, local, and pollinator-friendly species, and avoiding chemicals and pesticides, supports interactions between plants, microorganisms, and insects.
- Leaving some areas “wild,” rotating crops in vegetable gardens, harvesting rainwater, and sowing cover crops between growing seasons.
Together, these practices help build humus-rich soils that are more resilient to drought and extreme rainfall.
As consumers: Supporting soil health through everyday choices
Our food choices have a direct impact on soil health.
- Choosing products from sustainable farming systems — including organic and agroecological practices — supports methods that enhance soil organic matter, reduce erosion, and limit pollution.
- Buying local and seasonal products helps reduce pressure on soils while strengthening resilient regional food systems.
- Reducing food waste is equally important, as every discarded meal represents unnecessary use of soil, water, and energy.
- We can also diversify our diets, prioritise minimally processed foods, support short supply chains, and learn more about sustainability labels and farming practices.
These everyday choices help guide food systems toward practices that protect and restore soils.
At the local level: Acting collectively for soils
Soil health is a shared responsibility. We can engage locally by joining community gardens, urban greening projects, or collective composting initiatives. These actions contribute to restoring urban soils, improving water management, and strengthening social connections.
Participating in local planning discussions — particularly those related to land use and soil sealing — is another important step. Taking part in public consultations, supporting re-naturalisation projects, and advocating for the de-sealing of urban surfaces are concrete ways to protect soils in the long term. Supporting environmental organisations, joining tree-planting initiatives, and raising awareness in our communities also play a role.
Meeting the soil: Observing, learning, and getting involved
Restoring soil health also means reconnecting directly with soils. Observing soils in gardens, forests, or natural spaces is often the first step toward awareness. Looking at soil texture, colour, and smell, and noticing roots and soil organisms, reveals that living soil is a complex and essential ecosystem. Across Europe, citizens can go further by joining participatory science initiatives and contributing to soil monitoring — for example through programmes such as ECHO Soil.

title: Reimagining Our Future: Why pollinators need us now
text:
One-third of our bees, butterflies, and hoverflies are declining, and one in ten species in the EU faces extinction. Because pollinators underpin both our ecosystems and global food systems, their loss directly threatens our future.
For many young people, this reality feels overwhelming. The future can seem uncertain, and the scale of the problem, intimidating.
But what if the way forward begins with how we see the problem?
New way of thinking
Pollinator Ambassadors is a youth-led non-profit working to reverse pollinator decline. Co-founded by Nadine Schuller and me, the initiative combines art, science communication, and systems thinking to uncover local, actionable solutions to complex environmental challenges.
This work is also deeply connected to my own research and experience.
As a science communicator, beekeeper, and researcher at the University of Cambridge, my studies focus on how managed honeybees and wild bumblebees share landscapes in the UK. I hope my research will inform where and when we need to enhance landscapes to improve pollinator health.
Through working with young people across Europe, one insight has become clear: many environmental problems persist not only because of what we do, but because of how we think.
For example, prioritising profit over nature stems from a mindset that values short-term financial gain over long-term wellbeing. But if mindsets can contribute to the problem, they can also become part of the solution.
Understanding a 'wicked problem'
Pollinator decline is often described as a "wicked problem". This means it is complex, interconnected, and resistant to simple solutions.
We already understand many of its causes:
- Harmful pesticide use
- Climate change
- Habitat loss and land-use change
- Industrial agriculture
Addressing one issue often impacts another. For example, we need to produce food, but conventional agriculture depends heavily on pesticides - one of the main drivers of pollinator decline. At the same time, climate change increases our reliance on these same systems.
In short, everything is connected, and that makes change challenging.
Seeing the bigger picture
When problems feel overwhelming, systems thinking - understanding how parts interact within a whole to drive collective behaviour - offers a way forward.
Using tools like the Iceberg Model, we can look beyond visible symptoms and reshape the underlying structures of our society.
Facing environmental crises can lead to eco-anxiety, but creativity can transform that feeling into action.
Pollinator Ambassadors uses art as a tool for change, helping young people process emotions while imagining pollinator-friendly futures. Across the EU, participants in our workshops have created zines, exhibitions, and artistic projects that communicate both urgency and hope, bridging science and emotion in powerful ways.
10 Things You Can Do Right Now
One of the biggest threats to pollinators is the lack of habitat and food. Even without land or money, you can make a difference:
- Start conversations: Share why pollinators matter to you
- Plant a window box: Every flower provides vital nectar
- Create art: Express your vision for nature through a zine or sketch
- Connect: Join a local nature club
- Speak up: Ask retailers, like garden centres, to stop selling harmful pesticides
- Volunteer: Join community science projects such as ProPollSoil
- Explore: Organise a 'bee safari' to discover local species
- Green your workspace: Rally friends to start a garden at your school or office
- Let it grow: Ask your local council to reduce mowing to let wildflowers bloom
- Vote: Support policymakers who prioritise the environment

title: Small Waters, Big Impact: How to build a pond
text:
I work as an aquatic ecologist mainly in lentic waters (ponds, lakes, and wetlands), with a focus on the biodiversity and biological structure of these ecosystems and their response to global change, including climate change and pollution. My interest also extends to factors influencing freshwater biodiversity across continental gradients.
Ultimately, I aim to apply my research to solving conservation challenges. To this end, I place particular emphasis on transferring knowledge to European policy and implementation platforms.
I've been the coordinator of the European-funded PONDERFUL project, which explored how ponds and pond networks, so-called "pondscapes", can act as nature-based solutions to help society adapt to climate change, protect biodiversity, and provide clean water and other ecosystem services.
How to build a pond
Ponds are extremely important for biodiversity and ecosystem services, yet they are rapidly disappearing worldwide. Creating new ponds can help reverse this trend and support nature. Here are some key steps:
- Choose the right location 
Ideally, place the pond near existing ponds so species can reach it easily. Ensure access to water (groundwater, surface water, or rainwater) and aim for a balance of sun and shade. Avoid areas directly under trees that shed large amounts of leaves.
- Design for different depths 
Most pond organisms thrive in shallow water (20–50 cm), so include wide, gently sloping margins. Add some deeper areas (up to 1–2 m) to increase habitat diversity.
- Ensure water retention 
In clay soils or naturally wet areas, the pond may hold water on its own. Otherwise, install a waterproof liner, protected with sand or geotextile, and cover edges with soil and stones.
- Use appropriate plants 
Introduce aquatic plants from nearby wetlands to support natural colonisation. Avoid non-native or invasive species and check local regulations.
- Create shelter for wildlife 
Add rocks, logs, and natural materials around the pond to provide refuge for different species.
- Manage the pond over time 
Remove excessive vegetation or invasive species when needed to maintain a balanced ecosystem.
- Let nature do the work 
In most cases, a well-designed pond will naturally attract wildlife without further intervention.

title: Turn Your Garden into a Living Garden
text:
Every day, thousands of volunteers and a dedicated team of professionals team up to protect and restore our natural landscapes and their biodiversity.
My own personal mission is to get as many people as possible involved. I teach, lecture, guide, host a podcast and share my expertise and passion in weekly interviews on national radio.
Although protecting and restoring robust natural landscapes should be our main focus to preserve biodiversity, I have experienced that natural gardens can also be of great importance in our fragmented European landscapes.
Without really trying to get the most out of it, I've spotted over 700 animal species in my little garden, some of which are very rare.
Would you like to know my secret? Here’s my Top 7 garden hacks:
- Add water, large or small Birds need baths, bats fancy a drink, and many insects start their lives in the water. Even the smallest of ponds can give your garden a biodiversity boost. Do not fear a plague of mosquitoes. Most of them will be eaten by water beetles, damselflies and water striders.
- Give trees a chance Don’t be satisfied with just grass and flowerbeds. Do whatever you can to preserve old trees and plant new ones. In tiny urban gardens, climbers and ramblers against the wall will do just fine. This lush greenery is home to nesting birds and provides you with shade and a natural air conditioner.
- Prioritise native blooms Our native insects and flowers have been living together for thousands of years in an interdependent relationship. Every season has its own species. Early spring blooming willow catkins attract a myriad of pollinators, and in the midst of summer, meadow flowers do the same. The flower that gets the most bee species to visit is the dandelion.
- Respect the soil Don’t fertilise your soil! Poor soils have a rich biodiversity. Adapt your plant species to the soil, not the other way around. Be inspired by the species blooming in a nearby natural area. Trees and shrubs do like richer soil. Create a humus layer, using compost, autumn leaves and chopped wood. Hedgehogs will love this small-scale forest floor!
- Plant an edible garden Fruiting trees and shrubs prove to be great assets to natural gardens. Blossoms attract pollinators, and if you are willing to share your harvest, squirrels, trushes and dormice may thrive in your backyard.
- Become a landlord Provide extra housing for animals. A bat shelter, hedgehog home, bumblebee nestbox or a hotel for wild bees. There is, of course, a wide variety of birdhouses. Invite a robin to your hedge, a barn owl to the barn or even a stork upon your roof.
- Sing the lazy song Uncut grass, fallen leaves, dry plant stems, and dead wood are a true haven for crawling critters. Choose a hammock over a lawnmower or a lazy chair over a leaf blower.

title: Commission approves Bulgarian, German and Slovenian State aid schemes providing temporary electricity price relief for energy-intensive companies
text:
The European Commission has approved State aid schemes to provide temporary electricity price relief for energy-intensive companies in Bulgaria, Germany and Slovenia in line with the objectives of the Clean Industrial Deal. Through the condition to reinvest a significant share of the aid received in decarbonisation measures, these schemes will contribute to the transition towards a net-zero economy. The schemes were approved under the Clean Industrial Deal State Aid Framework (CISAF) adopted by the Commission on 25 June 2025.
The support measures
Bulgaria, Germany and Slovenia notified to the Commission, under the CISAF, schemes to provide temporary electricity price relief for companies in energy-intensive industries. The budgets of the schemes are €334 million for Bulgaria, €3.8 billion for Germany and €90 million for Slovenia.
The purpose of the schemes is to support energy-intensive companies by compensating them for a share of their electricity costs in the coming three years. The measures will be open to companies active in sectors with a significant risk of activities moving outside the EU to locations where environmental measures are absent or less ambitious. This risk depends on the electro-intensity of the sector in question and its openness to international trade. The sectors with a significant risk are listed in the 2022 guidelines on State aid for climate, environmental protection and energy.
The Commission found that the schemes are in line with the conditions set out in the CISAF. In particular:
The Bulgarian measure will run from 1 July 2025 to 30 June 2028. Bulgaria will pay the aid through electricity suppliers via a reduction on the beneficiaries' monthly electricity bill.
The German measure will run from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2028. Companies can apply for aid payments after the end of each year, when the electricity consumption and the average wholesale market price are known.
The Slovenian scheme will run from 1 January 2026 to 31 December 2028 and will pay out the aid twice a year based on expected electricity consumption.
The Commission concluded that the schemes are necessary, appropriate and proportionate to accelerate the transition towards a net-zero economy and facilitate the development of certain economic activities, which are of importance for the implementation of the Clean Industrial Deal. This is in line with Article 107(3)(c) of the Treaty on the Functioning of the EU and the conditions set out in the CISAF.
On this basis, the Commission approved the three aid measures under EU State aid rules.
Background
On 25 June 2025, the Commission adopted the CISAF to foster support measures in sectors which are key for the transition to a net-zero economy, in line with the Clean Industrial Deal.
The CISAF allows the following types of aid, which can be granted by Member States until 31 December 2030 in order to accelerate the green transition:
More information on the CISAF can be found online.
On 13 April 2026, the Commission launched a consultation for Member States on a Temporary Crisis Framework to address higher energy prices due to the Middle East crisis. This framework would complement the ample possibilities for Member States to design measures in line with existing EU State aid rules, including those under the CISAF.
For more information
The non-confidential versions of today's decisions will be made available under the case numbers SA.120414 (Bulgaria), SA.120495 (Germany), SA.120965 (Slovenia) in the State aid register on the Commission's competition website once any confidentiality issues have been resolved. New publications of State aid decisions on the internet and in the Official Journal are listed in the Competition Weekly e-News.

title: Stop Invasive Species and Restore Natural Balance
text:
Nature restoration is not something that only happens in protected areas; it often starts much closer to home. Along the Flemish coastline, I see every day how fragile our dune ecosystems are and how easily they can be disrupted.
Through my work in nature restoration, I focus particularly on tackling invasive non-native plant species that threaten our local coastal biodiversity.
One of the key initiatives I am involved in is the LIFE DUNIAS project, a large-scale effort to restore dune ecosystems along the Belgian coast. Together with multiple partners, and with support from the EU LIFE programme, we are removing invasive plant species to allow native vegetation to recover.
In most areas, we use heavy machinery to remove invasive species, as excavating and sifting the sand is the most efficient approach. While this may look drastic, it is essential to restore the natural balance and ensure the future of these unique landscapes.
Invasive species are one of the biggest challenges we face. Many of these plants were originally introduced through gardens and parks because of their attractive appearance. Over time, they escaped into nature - carried by wind, birds, or even through garden waste.
Climate change is only fueling the fire, helping certain species spread faster than ever. What looks like a harmless, attractive shrub in a garden can become a monoculture nightmare in the wild, choking out native plants and dismantling entire ecosystems.
You do not need to be a scientist or a land manager to make a difference.
How you can help
Everyone has a role to play in restoring nature. You do not need a degree in biology or to be a land manager to make a difference. Nature restoration is a shared responsibility, and it often comes down to small, daily choices.
1. Become an early warning system
Early detection is our best defence. If you’re in Belgium, you can help us spot outbreaks before they get out of control by logging observations on:
For those elsewhere in Europe, you can report sightings via the EASIN (European Alien Species Information Network). Your data allows us to act fast.
2. Make 'nature-friendly' choices at home
Many invasive plants are still sold in nurseries because of their flowers. By choosing native species for your garden, you provide a haven for local insects and birds rather than a launchpad for an invasion.
Never dump garden waste in natural areas. It might seem biodegradable, but it’s often full of seeds and roots that allow invasive species to establish and spread into dunes.
3. Join the community
Knowledge is power. By learning about your local environment and sharing what you know, we can collectively improve how we manage our environment.
Joining local nature groups or taking part in volunteer actions, such as community removal efforts, is a powerful way to contribute. These initiatives not only help restore ecosystems but also reconnect people with nature and with each other.
Through my work, I have seen that awareness is the first step toward action. Many invasive species problems originate from small, everyday decisions — but the same is true for solutions. If we make more conscious choices in our gardens, report what we see in nature, and work together at the local level, we can protect and restore our dunes.
Nature restoration is a shared responsibility. And sometimes, the most important step is simply recognising that what we plant, discard, or overlook today can shape the landscapes of tomorrow.

title: Ten EU countries exceeding SUPD collection targets
text:
The European Commission published the first report under the Single Use Plastics Directive (SUPD) on Thursday (16 April) based on data from EU Member States. The report shows several countries had already met some targets by 2022.
The report will be used as a baseline to measure:
- Member States’ compliance with the 2025 and 2030 binding targets for the separate collection of SUP beverage bottles
- Consumption of SUP food containers and beverage cups
- The amount of fishing gear containing plastic that is placed on the market and collected as waste
In 2022:
- 524,003 tonnes of SUP food containers (about 1.6 kg per person) and 152,037 tonnes of SUP beverage cups (about 0.5 kg per person) were sold in the EU. Subsequent reports will measure whether Member States have reduced the consumption of these products by 2026.
- The most common measures introduced by Member States to reduce the consumption of SUP food containers and beverage cups included economic instruments, such as extended producer responsibility (EPR) obligations and green public procurement instruments, as well as awareness campaigns and the promotion of sustainable alternatives.
- 71% of SUP beverage bottles were separately collected across the EU. Estonia, Poland, Finland, Germany, Denmark, Sweden, Lithuania, Croatia, Slovakia and Belgium have already met the 2025 target of 77%, with six of these countries already meeting the 2030 target of 90% (Estonia, Poland, Finland, Germany, Denmark and Sweden). Countries with high collection rates generally operate Deposit and Refund Systems (DRS).
- 22,900 tonnes of plastic-containing fishing gear were placed on the market, with around a third collected as waste.
Next steps
The Commission will continue to monitor Member States’ progress, based on their annual reporting on single-use plastics. These updates will track changes in consumption and collection, and evaluate the success of measures to reduce environmental impacts using the 2022 data as the baseline for future monitoring.
Background
The SUPD Directive targets the ten most commonly found single-use plastic products on European beaches, as well as plastic-containing fishing gear. It introduces measures for different categories of products, including those made entirely or partly from plastics.
Where affordable and easily available alternatives exist (such as paper), single-use plastic products have been banned: cotton bud sticks, cutlery, plates, stirrers, straws, balloon sticks, and food and beverage containers made of expanded polystyrene, as well as all products made of oxo-degradable plastics.
The EU aims to limit other single-use plastics through measures such as consumption reduction and the promotion of reusable alternatives.
The Directive sets specific rules for fishing gear containing plastics, including producer responsibility from creation to end-of-life, monitoring and reporting obligations, and national annual collection rates for recycling.

title: 360.come: Cultivating a sustainable future in Guimarães
text:
In the city of Guimarães, Portugal, the 360.come project is helping young people find the answers to pressing environmental questions.
Developed by the Landscape Laboratory, the project aims to inspire behavioural change by promoting healthier and more sustainable food choices, reducing food waste, and encouraging responsible production and consumption.
Through innovative communication and participatory science, it fosters environmental and scientific literacy, helping communities better understand the links between food, soil, and sustainable land use.
Turning lessons into action
Through a series of interactive sessions, more than 320 students from local schools explored these topics. Across 16 classes, 80 sessions were delivered that combined science, creativity, and real-world application. Key activities included:
- Footprint tracking: Students calculated their own ecological footprints to understand their personal impact on the planet.
- Waste monitoring: Participants actively monitored food waste in school canteens to identify areas for improvement.
- Urban gardening: Students experimented with sustainable practices, such as growing microgreens using recycled materials.
- Soil exploration: Classes focused on soil as a living system, observing the organisms essential for biodiversity and food production.
“We talked about biodiversity. We handled the soil and looked for living organisms. Later, we observed everything as a group using a microscope and a magnifying glass. I really liked the project. I learned that biodiversity is basically the centre of life,” said Samuel Duarte, a student at EB2/3 das Taipas School.
Beyond the classroom, 360.come acts as a bridge to the local economy. By advocating for shorter supply chains, the project highlights the work of traditional farmers who prioritise health over high-intensity yields.
“I have always worked in agriculture. We don’t practice intensive farming, but rather a more traditional approach to avoid herbicides and pesticides, because we all know they are not good for our health. We avoid chemicals as much as possible. The project addressed these issues and valued local producers.”
Francisco Teixeira, Local producer
The project goes beyond awareness, focusing on measurable behavioural change. A nearly 10% drop in food waste serves as a powerful testament to the project's ability to turn environmental literacy into tangible action.
By treating young people as active participants, Guimarães is ensuring that the future of its land and its food is in capable hands.

title: Bringing soil science to life for the next generation
text:
What if learning about soil could be as exciting as watching a story unfold?
That’s the idea behind Happy Toppy, a new initiative helping children discover the hidden world beneath their feet and understand why it matters.
Developed through the SOILSTORIES project (Empowering Rural Youth Through Soil Literacy), the initiative is working with young people in rural communities to turn complex soil science into practical knowledge and everyday awareness.
In Dağkadı Village in Bursa, Türkiye, around 110 primary and secondary school students took part in workshops to explore soil health. Using simple scientific methods, they analysed local soil samples - testing pH levels and key nutrients such as nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium - and learned how these affect crops, ecosystems, and food production.
But the project goes beyond science alone. By combining experimentation with storytelling, SOILSTORIES introduced characters like Happy Toppy, Wiggly Wiggy, and Zinny, helping students connect with the subject in a fun and memorable way. A documentary capturing the experience brings these learning moments to a wider audience.
Tackling a hidden challenge
The project addresses a real problem in agriculture: a lack of trust. In many rural areas, farmers can be hesitant to adopt new technology or share data. By focusing on children, who are essentially the future farmers, the initiative is building long-term change.
When students learn about soil health, they go home and talk to their parents about it. This creates a ripple effect of trust and new ideas within the wider farming community.
So far, the initiative has reached more than 700 children, including those from disadvantaged backgrounds, and continues to expand.
To support wider impact, the team has developed:
- A bilingual educational documentary (English and Turkish)
- A soil literacy toolkit for schools
- A growing online learning platform through the Happy Toppy YouTube channels
With over 11,000 combined subscribers and more than 600,000 video views, these digital platforms are helping bring soil education to a global audience.
Fresh agriculture discourse
At its core, the project is about making agriculture and environmental science more accessible and more appealing to young people.
Through regular videos, songs, and storytelling, Happy Toppy introduces topics such as soil health, biodiversity, and sustainable farming in ways that are easy to understand and engaging for children.
The long-term vision is to build soil trust circles, where young people and experienced farmers can exchange knowledge, combining traditional farming wisdom with modern digital skills and citizen science.
By making agriculture and environmental science fun and accessible through songs and stories, Happy Toppy is doing more than just teaching a lesson. It's helping a new generation feel proud of their farming roots and giving them the tools to look after the land for years to come.

title: How 'Astrotourism' is helping rural Albania
text:
Albania’s night skies are among the clearest in Europe, yet few people were taking the time to appreciate them. Star Campers Albania is changing that by bringing people together to explore the universe while protecting the natural world.
Since 2021, the project has grown from a small group of friends into a community of over 1,200 participants who travel to some of the country’s most remote and beautiful landscapes.
Activities first took place in Shebenik National Park and along the historic Via Egnatia route, but have since expanded across Albania. During the 2025 summer season alone, more than 800 visitors joined multi-day camping experiences under some of Europe’s most untouched night skies.
The idea behind Star Campers was simple. What began as a group of friends - astronomers, musicians, and mountain lovers - sharing nights around a campfire has grown into a vibrant community built on curiosity, connection, and respect for nature.
Today, participants use telescopes, laser pointers, and digital sky-mapping tools to explore the universe while learning about light pollution, biodiversity protection, and responsible outdoor practices. By shifting the focus from daytime tourism to the night sky, the initiative offers a fresh perspective on sustainability and environmental awareness.
Supporting the Local Economy
One of the most important parts of the project is its focus on rural communities. Instead of mass tourism that often ignores local people, Star Campers works directly with:
- Local guides: Using the expertise of people who know the land best.
- Guesthouses and small businesses: Ensuring tourists' money stays in remote villages, providing a sustainable income for families.
The initiative has also expanded to include Star Campers Kids, introducing children and young people to astronomy, nature exploration, and environmental responsibility through hands-on outdoor learning. Safe, structured programmes ensure that young participants can explore and learn in a supportive environment.
Guided by values such as putting nature first, fostering learning, and prioritising community over crowds, the project offers a replicable model for green skills development. It shows how small-scale, meaningful experiences can inspire people to value and protect the natural world.
By linking astronomy, environmental awareness, and local engagement, Star Campers Albania is helping to build a new generation that understands and connects with Nature.

title: How a forest classroom is planting hope in Ukraine
text:
In the wake of conflict and devastation, the city of Bucha is finding new ways to heal and rebuild. An inspiring initiative to emerge from this process is the Bucha Forest Classroom - a nature-based learning space.
The events of 2022 left a deep mark on Bucha. Following the early stages of the Russian invasion, the city faced the immense challenge of rebuilding both its infrastructure and its sense of community. Restoring education quickly became a priority.
The Forest Classroom grew out of the wider Bucha School project, launched in summer 2022 after a Lithuanian business group donated land for a new school.
“The idea is to create a smaller, nature-integrated educational space - a ‘little brother’ to the larger school - using sustainable, innovative materials.”
Aivaras Karalius, Project’s Coordinator
Built to fit the environment
Located in a public park, the Bucha Forest Classroom is designed as a multi-functional space that integrates education and nature. And it's built to work with nature, not against it. Rather than using concrete, the design uses natural materials like:
- Better materials: Rather than using heavy concrete, the classroom is built with sustainable straw panels and natural wood.
- Solar power: The building uses solar panels and energy-efficient systems to minimise its environmental impact.
- Hands-on learning: There is a greenhouse and garden beds where students grow plants, helping them learn about nature by actually working with it.
For many children in Bucha, the last few years have been incredibly stressful. The Forest Classroom acts as a green refuge. It's a calm, quiet environment that helps students focus and provides a sense of peace that is hard to find in a standard classroom.
The children were not just handed the keys, either. They helped come up with the ideas for the space and picked out some of the materials. This involvement fosters a sense of ownership and responsibility, encouraging students to value and care for their environment. It also introduces them to concepts such as regenerative design and sustainable living in a tangible way.
The classroom is expected to host more than 12,000 children through environmental education programmes, offering opportunities to explore biodiversity, sustainability, and ecological thinking.
A global effort
Above all, the project stands as a strong example of international cooperation, coordinated by the Support Fund for Bucha School and the Bucha municipality, with contributions from Lithuanian and Ukrainian partners.
In total, 43 companies, 118 volunteers, and over 300 private donors contributed to the initiative, mobilising around €200,000 in funding, materials, and equipment.
The Bucha Forest Classroom is more than a single project, it's a symbol of resilience and a model for rebuilding sustainably.
By combining education, nature, and community participation, this approach shows that even after a disaster, it's possible to build something thoughtful, sustainable, and full of hope.

title: How a tourism project is helping protect nature and jobs in Colombia
text:
Colombia is home to some of the most diverse plant and animal life on Earth. However, the local people living in these areas often see very little of the money that tourists bring in. In Latin America, it's estimated that local communities receive less than 5% of the total income generated by tourism.
In Colombia’s Chocó region, one of the richest ecosystems on Earth, this imbalance is especially visible.
A project called CHECK - a regenerative tourism and territorial innovation initiative - has been working since 2021 to change this balance. They want to show that travel can be used to protect nature and help locals earn a steady living.
Learning while enjoying
Instead of traditional tours where visitors just look at the scenery and leave, CHECK embeds learning in biodiverse territories through locally led checkpoints.
At these spots, the focus is on:
- Hands-on learning: Travellers and locals learn about the environment together.
- Research: Regular people help gather data on local wildlife (sometimes called "citizen science").
- Local leadership: The projects are run by the people who actually live there, not outside companies.
Since its launch, CHECK has worked with 200 local operators across 20 destinations, involving more than 1,500 travellers and learners in regenerative tourism practices.
In Arusí, on Colombia’s Pacific coast, CHECK’s 'Jardín del Mar' or 'Sea Garden' checkpoint shows how this approach works on the ground. The area is famous for its coral ecosystems, sea turtle nesting sites, and humpback whale habitats, and the initiative brings together environmental education and community-led conservation.
More than 60 children and 50 local volunteers are involved in marine education and protection activities, learning about biodiversity, citizen science, and sustainable tourism. The programme has also created new income opportunities linked to responsible travel, helping communities benefit directly from protecting their natural environment.
The model follows a structured process - from local co-design and implementation to impact measurement and community-led management - ensuring that projects are both effective and locally owned.
Building future skills
Beyond conservation and hosting tourists, CHECK focuses on strengthening local skills and livelihoods. By working with academia, NGOs, and private sector partners, the initiative supports training in sustainable tourism, environmental management, and entrepreneurship.
This approach increases community participation in ecosystem protection while creating long-term economic opportunities. It also aligns with Colombia’s broader community tourism strategy, contributing to more inclusive and sustainable development in remote regions.
The initiative demonstrates how tourism, when designed carefully, can provide the funding and the people-power needed to save endangered habitats while making life better for the people who call those places home.

title: Protecting the Americas' birds by preserving its salt lakes
text:
You may be surprised to hear this, but birds are unaware of borders. Every year, thousands of them fly incredible distances between North and South America.
To survive this journey, these birds rely on vital salt lakes that act as crucial pit stops where they can eat and recover as they travel continental migratory flyways.
Protecting these ecosystems supports both local biodiversity and the wider ecological networks that sustain migratory bird populations across the Americas.
Experience Ambientalia is a project that connects the young people living near these lakes. It helps students in Argentina and the United States work together to protect the water and birds they share.
Even though they live thousands of miles apart, these youngsters in the U.S. and Argentina are looking at the same birds. The project currently runs at four major lake systems: Laguna Mar Chiquita and Laguna de los Pozuelos in Argentina, and Mono Lake and Great Salt Lake in the United States.
Although geographically distant, these locations are connected through shared migratory bird pathways and Experience Ambientalia's youth-led conservation learning activities.
By focusing on these four spots, the project creates a chain of protection along the path the birds fly.
Learning by doing
This is not just about sitting in a classroom. The project is built on getting students outside and involved in their own communities.
- Local projects: Students have started 76 community-based environmental projects linked to the protection of saline lake ecosystems.
- Youth leadership: More than 800 students have taken part, learning how to speak up for their local ecosystems and take care of the land.
- Exchanges: Participating chapters have also coordinated more than 20 parallel activities aligned with international environmental dates and organised three exchange visits between participating lake regions.
By teaching young people why these habitats matter, Experience Ambientalia is building a network of future leaders who understand that protecting a lake in their own backyard helps the whole hemisphere.
Since 2021, this initiative has shown that environmental protection is most effective when it's personal. When a student in Argentina knows that the bird they are watching will soon be seen by a student in Utah or California, it creates a powerful sense of responsibility.
It proves that you don't have to be a scientist or a politician to make a difference, you just need to care about your home and stay connected to others doing the same.

title: Saving land in Papua New Guinea through trees and coffee
text:
In the Daulo District of Papua New Guinea, most of the 70,000 residents live off the land. But for years, that land has been under threat. Frequent floods, landslides, and soil erosion have made it harder for families to grow enough food to eat or coffee to sell.
In 2019, a local group called the Daulo Commodities Cooperative Society (DCCSL) was formed to help farmers fight back. Their approach is simple: use nature to protect the soil.
The cooperative teaches a method called agroforestry, where trees are planted alongside food crops. This helps the community in several ways:
- Stronger soil: Tree roots act like an anchor, holding the dirt in place to prevent landslides and erosion.
- Better coffee: Planting shade trees in coffee gardens protects the plants from harsh weather and improves the quality of the beans.
- Healthier crops: The cooperative provides seedlings, tools, and soil testing to help farmers grow more food for their families and better produce for the market.
Skills for all
The project is not just about plants, it’s also about people. The cooperative provides training in modern farming and business skills so that farmers can get a fair price for their hard work.
This includes everyone from women, youth, persons living with disabilities, widows, and orphans. Women take part in training, farming activities, and small business development, and are supported to participate alongside men in community programmes and decision-making processes.
The results in Daulo have been so clear that even people in neighbouring districts are starting to notice and request the same training.
What started as a small group in 2019 is now expanding training activities with demonstration sites and practical learning in nursery management, onion fermentation, tree planting, and coffee extension across three provinces.
By teaching farmers how to work with the environment rather than just on it, the cooperative is helping families build a life that can survive the changing climate.

title: Saving the Amazon: Indigenous women leading from within
text:
The Amazon rainforest is one of the most important places on Earth, but it's under constant threat. For the people who live there, the danger is personal.
Cutting down trees, mining pollution, and changing weather patterns are making it harder for communities to survive. These challenges are also accelerating the loss of Indigenous knowledge passed down through generations.
In response, Indigenous women across the Amazon are emerging as key leaders in the fight against climate change.
They are supported by the Amazonia Indigenous Women’s Fellowship (AIWF), a programme launched in 2021 to provide the funding and training needed to lead environmental projects rooted in traditional knowledge.
Ancient knowledge, modern problems
Since the project began, it has focused on practical ways to protect the forest and the people who live there:
- Broad impact: The fellowship has supported more than 115 projects and directly benefited over 4,200 people.
- Significant investment: Since its launch, €1.36 million has gone directly into the hands of Indigenous women-led initiatives.
- Key focus areas: These projects span the Amazon and focus on reforestation, food sovereignty, and territorial management.
In Bolivia, Fulvia Medina is working with women across 23 different communities. Together, they are preserving traditional weaving techniques while creating sustainable ways to earn an income. Her work ensures that these cultural traditions remain a viable way for families to support themselves.
In Colombia, Paola Margarita Chindoy is focusing on the connection between generations. By bringing young people and elders together, she is helping to protect ancestral knowledge and defend Indigenous territories from outside threats. These efforts ensure that the wisdom passed down through centuries is not lost to modern environmental pressures.
As global attention turns toward inclusive climate solutions, this initiative highlights an important reality: Indigenous women are not only protecting the Amazon, they are helping define its future.
By supporting these leaders, the programme ensures that the people who know the forest best are the ones shaping its recovery.

title: Trees Under the Microscope: Bringing science and nature together in Armenia
text:
What if you could see an entire hidden world inside a single leaf?
In Armenia, a project called Trees Under the Microscope is helping children discover how trees live, breathe, and communicate. As one young participant puts it: "Once you see this, you don't need to be told not to cut a tree, you already understand that it's alive."
Using microscopes, participants examine different tree species, prepare their own samples, and observe the cellular structures that make each tree unique. Through this process, they gain a deeper understanding of Armenia’s rich natural environment.
“We had many adventures while piloting the project,” says founder Nelli Yeghoyan.
“Imagine the most exciting moment, when suddenly heavy rain begins. With only one umbrella, the children protected the microscope and refused to stop the workshop. Or imagine a line of young ‘scientists’ waiting by the only microscope, unable to wait even a minute to observe the samples they had prepared with their own hands.”
Despite such challenges, the pilot phase proved highly successful. Nearly 200 children took part, and for around 84% of them, it was their first time using a microscope. The experience left a lasting impression.
Teachers have since reported increased interest in science subjects, improved academic performance, and a stronger sense of care for the trees in schoolyards. The project not only supports formal education but also makes science accessible and engaging for children of all backgrounds.
“The goal is not necessarily for children to become scientists. What matters most is that they develop a science-based understanding of nature and truly understand what is happening inside it - especially within trees - and why these remarkable living organisms are so important.”
Nelli Yeghoyan, Trees Under the Microscope Founder
So far, more than 700 children have participated, including displaced children from Artsakh and children from rehabilitation centres. With support from partner foundations, the project has expanded its equipment and capacity, enabling more outdoor learning activities.
“It feels like real magic to see how excited the children become, how their eyes shine, how they discuss and share their discoveries,” Nelli explains. “It's a joy to watch them feel proud of their work and take home their own unique creations.”
Looking ahead, the project aims to reach 1,000 children and establish an EcoEducation Garden, a dedicated learning space featuring Armenia’s endemic tree species.
“I dream that one day every child will see Armenia’s trees as they have never seen them before and learn to value and protect our nature,” she says.
Because when children understand nature, they are far more likely to protect it. And that is where real change begins.

title: Sow, Grow, Unite: A garden for every generation in Gozo
text:
In the grounds of the Gozo General Hospital, Malta, a first-of-its-kind project has taken root. The Sow, Grow, Unite Community Garden is a shared outdoor space where students, parents, hospital staff, and elderly residents work side-by-side.
Developed by schools and local partners, the garden isn't just about plants, it’s also about how a living classroom has been designed to support both the environment and the well-being of the community.
The heart of the garden is intergenerational collaboration. It's a place where people of different ages meet to share what they know, allowing younger students to learn traditional skills from elderly residents while everyone shares the responsibility of looking after the crops.
By working together on a shared goal, participants have built new friendships that strengthen the local community.
The garden also gives families a dedicated place to spend time together outdoors. By participating in the process of growing their own food, parents and children can reconnect with nature and learn about the importance of seasonal, local produce.
This shared interaction has turned a simple green space into a hub for student-led engagement in sustainability.
Farming with nature
The garden follows strict sustainability rules to make sure it helps the local ecosystem rather than harming it.
- Natural methods: All food is grown without pesticides, using permaculture principles that work well in the Maltese climate.
- Zero-waste: The garden uses communal composting for organic waste and upcycled materials whenever possible.
- Smart resources: Water is used responsibly, and participants are encouraged to reach the site on foot or by bicycle to help reduce its carbon footprint.
The garden is filled with seasonal fruits, vegetables, and local plants that attract bees and butterflies. Because it's located at a hospital, it serves as a constant reminder of the link between fresh food, nature, and health.
The project has also sparked a spirit of sharing. Participants regularly exchange seeds, tools, and gardening tips. To celebrate this, the garden recently launched its own recipe book, featuring simple, healthy meals made from the local ingredients harvested right on-site.
This initiative shows what happens when schools and hospitals work together with the community. It has turned a simple green space into a hub for student-led engagement in sustainability.
With plans to bring in even more partners, the garden will continue to grow as a space where everyone is welcome to learn, plant, and unite.

title: Blooming, beautiful, and chemical-free: Great gardens can also be pollinator havens
text:
I’m Barbara Berardi, I work for Pesticide Action Network Europe. PAN is dedicated to protecting human health and biodiversity from the harmful effects of pesticides and to championing safer alternatives.
Pesticide contamination is everywhere, in soils, surface water and groundwater, vegetation, air. This contamination contributes significantly to the decline of insects, pollinators, farmland birds, soil organisms, and aquatic biodiversity. Such impacts undermine ecosystem functioning, agricultural resilience, and long-term food security.
But reducing chemical pesticides is possible.
Practical experience from farmers across Europe shows that pesticide use can be substantially reduced without affecting farm profitability
Pesticide-free urban green spaces, such as public parks and school grounds, also support the recovery of pollinator populations, while safeguarding human health. Some European cities are already putting this into practice. Paris has been entirely pesticide-free for several years, in fact pesticides have been banned in all towns and cities in France. Similar policies have been implemented in Denmark, Belgium, the Netherlands, Sweden and Luxembourg.
Private gardens and even balconies can be refuges for pollinators and other insects. Even the smallest outdoor space can become part of a living network that supports nature.
Beneficial arthropods, such as pollinators and natural enemies of pests (e.g. ladybirds, lacewings, hoverflies) keep pest populations in check for free, provided that they are protected against harmful pesticides.
What you can do
Plant for diversity: Include a variety of flowering plants that bloom at different times across the season. This ensures a continuous supply of nectar and pollen - not only for bees and butterflies, but also for hoverflies and parasitic wasps, whose larvae prey on aphids and other pests. Some plants - such as marigolds - attract a broad spectrum of insects. Others, such as certain salvias, support honey bees and bumblebees, while dwarf zinnias are particularly appealing to butterflies
Choose local plants: Local pollinators have evolved alongside these plants, adapting to their specific characteristics, such as bloom cycles, shapes and colors. Native species are better suited to local conditions, requiring less maintenance and care.
Grow herbs: Basil, rosemary, thyme…Besides being a delicious addition to your recipes, when allowed to flower they become valuable food sources for pollinators, and provide natural pest control. Basil planted near tomatoes is known to deter hornworms, thrips and aphids. Rosemary helps repel a range of common garden pests. Borage (Borago officinalis) flowers draw bees and pest-hunting wasps, while the plant itself acts as a deterrent to hornworms.
Go wild for wildflowers: A border strip of mixed native wildflowers along the edge of your beds acts as a reservoir from which beneficial insects can spread into vegetable plots when pests appear. In a community garden, a seed swap is a simple and effective way to multiply these plants across the neighbourhood — the more people grow them, the greater the collective benefit.
Provide water: Pollinators also need safe access to water and sheltered resting spots. Shallow water containers are preferable, to avoid drowning small insects. Butterflies benefit from calm, wind-protected areas to rest between flights. Many solitary bees require undisturbed spots to nest and overwinter. Even a small pile of dead wood or a simple insect hotel can make a difference.
Most importantly, avoid chemical pesticides. They are harmful to the very insects you are trying to attract. A well-watered balanced garden does not need much human intervention. Where necessary, use targeted, natural methods instead, such as manually removing pests by hand or with water, or applying a mild, fragrance-free soapy spray directly to the affected area.
Pollinator-friendly spaces form lifelines through the urban landscape that allow bees, butterflies and their allies to move, feed and survive. These uncontaminated refuges and food sources help transform the city into a healthier, greener and better place where nature can thrive.
We've gathered tips from around Europe as part of the #ForOurPlanet 2026 campaign. Learn how you can make a difference with a few simple actions at home, or how to get out and work with your community and others to help bring back nature.
