title: Commission unconditionally approves Arla's acquisition of DMK and DOC
text:
The European Commission has unconditionally approved, under the EU Merger Regulation, the proposed acquisition by Arla Foods amba ('Arla') of Deutsches Milchkontor eG ('DMK') and Drents Overijsselse Coöperatie Kaas U.A.('DOC'). The Commission concluded that the transaction would raise no competition concerns in the European Economic Area ('EEA').
Arla, DMK and DOC are dairy cooperatives that collect raw milk from their associated farmers and process it into a wide range of dairy products, which they sell in a number of countries in the EEA and beyond. Such products include fresh milk, butter, yoghurt, cream, cheese or whey-based ingredients.
The Commission's investigation
The Commission investigated the impact of the transaction in a large number of markets in the EEA. In particular, it looked at the market for raw milk procurement from farmers in Germany, and the markets for the supply of dairy products and whey-based ingredients to retailers, wholesalers and industrial customers, in Denmark, Finland, Germany, the Netherlands and Sweden. Based on its market investigation, the Commission found that the transaction, as notified, would not significantly reduce competition in these markets.
More specifically:
The Commission therefore concluded that the proposed transaction would raise no competition concerns, and cleared the transaction unconditionally.
Companies and products
Arla, headquartered in Denmark, is a vertically integrated dairy cooperative of over 7.000 farmers across Denmark, Sweden, the UK, Germany, Belgium, Luxembourg, and the Netherlands. Arla collects raw milk from its associated farmers and processes it into a wide range of dairy products, including fresh milk, butter, yoghurt, cream and cheese. It also operates an ingredients business through its subsidiary Arla Foods Ingredients Group P/S, which focuses on the development and production of milk- and whey-based nutrition solutions and ingredients. Arla sells its products globally and has production facilities in a number of countries.
DMK eG, headquartered in Germany, is a vertically integrated dairy cooperative of approximately 4.000 German dairy farmers. DMK collects raw milk from its associated farmers, which it then supplies to DMK Deutsches Milchkontor GmbH ('DMK GmbH'), a dairy company based in Germany. DMK eG owns 90% of the shares in DMK GmbH, and the remaining 10% of shares are held by DOC. DMK GmbH is the operating company of DMK eG and DOC, responsible for processing the milk from all their associated farmers into a wide range of dairy products, including basic milk products, cheese, baby food, ice cream, and dairy ingredients. DMK GmbH sells its products globally and has production facilities in a number of countries.
DOC, headquartered in the Netherlands, is a dairy cooperative of approximately 600 dairy farmers across the Netherlands and Germany. DOC collects milk from its associated farmers, which it then supplies to DMK GmbH for further processing into a wide range of dairy products.
Merger control rules and procedure
The transaction was notified to the Commission on 17 April 2026.
The Commission has the duty to assess mergers and acquisitions involving companies with a turnover above certain thresholds (see Article 1 of the EU Merger Regulation) and to prevent concentrations that would significantly impede effective competition in the EEA or any substantial part of it.
The vast majority of notified mergers do not pose competition problems and are cleared after a routine review. From the moment a transaction is notified, the Commission generally has 25 working days to decide whether to grant approval (Phase I) or to start an in-depth investigation (Phase II).
For more information
More information will be available on the Commission's competition website, in the public case register under the case number M.12115.

title: Video message for roundtable discussion on LNG & Shipping organised by CBS Alumni Club and Columbia Global Energy Centre
text:
"Check against delivery"
Ladies and gentlemen,
I have been asked to present the EU perspective on the closure of the Strait of Hormuz. But first, allow me to welcome that finally after month and a half, the Strait was opened at least for the course of the ceasefire. Because no matter where you are in the world, we are all impacted. The only way to move forwards is diplomacy, and I add my voice to the many others calling for an end to hostilities, and a return to permanent freedom of navigation. As I speak, energy supply is not a problem in Europe. Yet at least. Member States' oil and gas emergency stocks are full, and we are prepared if they are needed. But high prices are a problem. And not just in Europe. The EU imports most of its energy, making us vulnerable. But when global oil and gas prices increase, consumers elsewhere also feel it. Prices in the US have risen less steeply, because of domestic production and energy exports. For Europe, shipping is an energy lifeline. Oil, LNG and refined fuels such as diesel, jet fuel and bunker fuel arrive primarily by sea. Shipping also connects producers and consumers across continents. The global dimension is particularly visible in major producers' exports. The rapid growth of US LNG and oil exports in recent years, for example, has depended heavily on internationally active fleets, including European vessels. The current crisis underlines what we have been saying for some time about Europe's reliance on imported energy. Dependency makes us vulnerable. And we cannot afford to be vulnerable. We need to continue diversifying our energy supply, rapidly step up the production of alternatives fuels within the EU and transition away from fossil fuels. Actually, the maritime sector enables diversification. It allows us to source crude oil, petroleum products and LNG from a range of suppliers, to redirect cargoes across regions, and to avoid excessive reliance on any single route or region. LNG has a growing role in Europe's energy mix. This is only possible due to port infrastructure and shipping, supported by strong transatlantic cooperation. The US has rapidly become our first LNG supplier – and Europe is the US' largest LNG customer by far. In fact, energy is central in the EU-US trade deal. And record-breaking volumes of energy now flow across the Atlantic. Last year, the EU imported 76 billion cubic metres of US LNG, up from 45 billion cubic metres in 2024. I see real potential for further growth this year and next, as we implement our REPowerEU strategy. In fact, we recently signed several long-term LNG import agreements with the US. The EU-US trade deal is critical to ensuring the EU's energy security while the EU accelerates the full and permanent phase out of Russian fossil fuels.
Ladies and gentlemen, when chokepoints come under pressure, the importance of shipping is immediately clear. Energy security is not only about access to resources, but also about the capacity to transport them safely and reliably. This capacity is not infinite, however. Constraints in specialised tanker segments, including LNG carriers, can influence how quickly, and at what scale, flows can be redirected, particularly in times of crisis. The current crisis also highlights practical limits. Longer voyages, rerouting, war-risk conditions, and higher insurance and freight costs reduce the availability of vessels and increase the delivered cost of energy, even when supply exists. From the European perspective, the conclusion is clear. A resilient shipping sector is not only vital for Europe's own energy security. It's also a bedrock of international trade, our partners' exports, and energy markets that function in times of geopolitical stress. Thank you
